questions.stem: Why does Matching Pennies have no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium?
options: In every pure profile one player gains by switching
The payoffs are equal in every cell
There are too many strategies to compare
questions.explanation: Whatever pure pair is played, the loser wants to switch, so no pure profile is stable (Slide 2).
questions.hint: Pick any cell and ask who wants to move.

questions.stem: In a mixed-strategy equilibrium, each player chooses probabilities that…
options: Make the other player indifferent between their pure strategies
Maximise their own chance of winning each round
Match the other player's probabilities exactly
Minimise the total payoff of the game
questions.explanation: This is the indifference principle: if the other player weren't indifferent, they would switch to their better pure strategy (Slide 4).
questions.hint: What stops the other player from switching?

options: Every finite game has at least one Nash equilibrium, possibly mixed
Every game has a pure-strategy Nash equilibrium
Every Nash equilibrium is Pareto optimal
Every game has exactly one Nash equilibrium
questions.explanation: Nash (1950) showed that every finite game has at least one equilibrium, which may require mixed strategies (Slide 5).
